title: Five Great Red Grapes
quiz.0.question: Which grape is called the "King of Italy" and makes Barolo and Barbaresco?
quiz.0.explanation: Nebbiolo is Italy's greatest red grape, used for top wines such as Barolo and Barbaresco.
quiz.1.question: What is Barbera's main characteristic?
quiz.1.explanation: Barbera's distinctive combination of low tannin and high acidity makes it ideal for everyday drinking and food.

slides.1.title: 🏆 The Five Great Red Grapes at a Glance
slides.1.content:
Five grapes spanning Italy from north to south, from Piemonte's fog-loving Nebbiolo to Sicily's sun-drenched Nero d'Avola, covering the full flavour spectrum from top collector's wines to everyday drinking

👑 Nebbiolo — King of Italy

Piemonte's fog grape, with very high acidity + very high tannin; pale garnet in colour yet astonishingly powerful. Barolo (powerful) / Barbaresco (elegant), ageing 10-30 years.

🌟 Sangiovese + 💜 Barbera — The Twin Stars of Tuscany & Piemonte

Sangiovese: Italy's most widely planted (high acid, medium-high tannin, Chianti/Brunello), versatile, 5-30 years. Barbera: the everyday star (high acid, low tannin, easy and versatile, Barbera d'Asti), 2-8 years.

🍷 Montepulciano + 🌑 Nero d'Avola — Southern Characters

Montepulciano: Abruzzo's value choice (medium tannin, medium acid, full), 3-10 years. Nero d'Avola: king of Sicily (medium-high tannin, medium acid, rich and Mediterranean), 5-15 years.

slides.2.title: 👑 Nebbiolo — King of Italy
slides.2.content:
The "fog grape" (nebbia = fog), Italy's greatest red grape — a paradox: very high tannin + very high acidity, yet a pale garnet colour, needing 10-30 years to show its true face

🎨 Grape Profile

Colour: pale garnet with a brick-orange rim, turning brick-red with age (light in appearance, very powerful in substance)

Aromas: young: red cherry, rose, violet
aged: truffle, leather, tar, dried rose (supremely complex)

Palate: very high tannin (very astringent when young), very high acidity, medium to full body, 13.5-15%

Regions: Piemonte (the Langhe hills, Roero, and Ghemme and Gattinara in the north), also Lombardy's Valtellina

🍷 Key Wines & Food

Barolo DOCG: the "king of wines", powerful, calcareous marl soils, spanning 11 villages, ageing 10-30 years

Barbaresco DOCG: the "queen of wines", elegant, calcareous marl soils, opening earlier than Barolo, ageing 8-25 years

Roero DOCG / Langhe Nebbiolo DOC: lighter and more approachable, the best introduction to Nebbiolo; Gattinara and Ghemme in the north are leaner and finer

Food: truffle risotto, braised beef (brasato), game, aged Parmigiano

Ageing advice: wait at least 5-10 years; it truly opens up after 20

slides.3.title: 🌟 Sangiovese — The Soul of Tuscany
slides.3.content:
"Blood of Jupiter" (Sanguis Jovis), Italy's most widely planted red grape — high acid and medium-high tannin, covering the fullest quality spectrum from everyday Chianti to Brunello that ages for decades

🎨 Grape Profile

Colour: medium ruby with purple or brick tints, moderately transparent

Aromas: young: sour cherry, red berries, plum, tomato leaf, herbs
aged: leather, aged spice, dried fruit, tobacco

Palate: medium to high tannin (firm), high acidity, medium to full body, 12.5-14.5%

Status in Italy: the most planted variety, grown throughout the country, at its finest in Tuscany

🍷 Key Wines & Food

Brunello di Montalcino DOCG: 100% Sangiovese, aged at least 5 years by law and able to age for decades, one of Italy's greatest wines

Chianti Classico DOCG: 80%+ Sangiovese, the Gallo Nero rooster seal, from everyday to fine Riserva

Vino Nobile DOCG: Sangiovese (locally Prugnolo Gentile), from the Tuscan town of Montepulciano

Food: pasta with tomato sauce, roast chicken, steak (bistecca fiorentina), pecorino cheese, pizza

slides.4.title: 💜 Barbera — The Everyday Star
slides.4.content:
Italy's everyday star and Piemonte's most widely planted red grape — the delicious paradox of high acid and low tannin: refreshing rather than astringent, full of fruit, and one of the best values in Italian red wine

🎨 Grape Profile

Colour: deep purple-red, intense and slow to fade

Aromas: black cherry, blackberry, plum, violet, liquorice
oaked versions: vanilla, toasted nuts, coffee

Palate: low to medium tannin (smooth, not astringent), high acidity (fresh and lively), medium to full body, 12.5-14%

Personality: high acid + low tannin = the most versatile red on the Italian table, enjoyable young

🍷 Key Wines & Food

Barbera d'Asti DOCG: province of Asti; the Superiore version is more complex, and the top Nizza became a separate DOCG in 2014

Barbera d'Alba DOC: the Langhe, next to Barolo/Barbaresco vineyards; oaked versions are richer

Barbera del Monferrato DOC: the Monferrato hills, easy everyday wines, great value

Food: salumi, stews, tomato dishes, pizza, grilled food — naturally versatile and stress-free

slides.5.title: 🍷 Montepulciano — King of Value
slides.5.content:
Abruzzo's central-Italian standard-bearer, ⚠️ a name trap you must learn — "Montepulciano d'Abruzzo" is a grape name; "Vino Nobile di Montepulciano" is a Tuscan place name + Sangiovese! Completely different

🎨 Grape Profile

Colour: deep purple-red, nearly opaque, extremely intense

Aromas: black cherry, plum, blackberry, dark chocolate, spice

Palate: medium tannin (smooth), medium acidity, full body, 12.5-14%

⚠️ Name trap: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo = red wine from the Montepulciano grape grown in Abruzzo; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano = Sangiovese red wine from the Tuscan town of Montepulciano (a completely different grape!)

🍷 Key Wines & Food

Montepulciano d'Abruzzo DOC: Abruzzo's most important red, full and fruity, excellent value

Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo DOC: a deep-coloured rosé from the same grape, called "Italy's most serious rosé"

Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane DOCG: the top version from the province of Teramo, with ageing potential

Food: roast lamb (agnello), barbecue, stews (guazzetto), Italian sausages — hearty and satisfying

slides.6.title: 🌑 Nero d'Avola — King of Sicily
slides.6.content:
The king of Sicily, a wine of the sun — the hot Mediterranean climate creates the richest, fullest reds, with black fruit, chocolate and spice; southern Italy's most important red grape

🎨 Grape Profile

Colour: deep ruby to deep red, very intense

Aromas: black cherry, blackberry, prune, dark chocolate, cinnamon, clove

Palate: medium-high tannin, medium acidity (lower than northern grapes), full and rich body, 13-15%

Heat tolerance: a heat- and drought-tolerant grape suited to Sicily's hot, dry climate; in the past it was mostly exported in bulk to deepen the colour of wines from other regions

🍷 Key Wines & Food

Nero d'Avola (single varietal): the most common in Sicily, from easy fruity styles to complex oaked versions

Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG: Sicily's only DOCG, a Nero d'Avola + Frappato blend, elegant and complex, with good examples able to age

Modern revival: quality has risen greatly since the 1990s, and it is now southern Italy's red grape with the most international attention

Food: grilled and braised meats, grilled tuna, caponata (sweet-and-sour aubergine), aged pecorino

slides.7.title: 📊 The Five Grapes Compared
slides.7.content:
From structure to choosing a bottle — understanding how the five grapes relate to each other is the most important foundation for getting into Italian red wine

💪 Highly Structured Grapes (high tannin + high acid)

Nebbiolo: very high tannin + very high acid, the longest ageing (10-30 years), for special occasions

Sangiovese: medium-high tannin + high acid, widely used (5-30 years), for dinners and entertaining

Traits: high acidity supports long ageing; natural partners for tomato and red-meat dishes

Note: can be too astringent when young — drink with food or wait for ageing

🍷 Smooth, Easy-Drinking Grapes (low-medium tannin)

Barbera: low tannin + high acid, the easiest and most versatile (2-8 years), good value, the everyday first choice

Montepulciano: medium tannin + medium acid, full and fruity (3-10 years), excellent value, perfect for barbecue

Nero d'Avola: medium-high tannin + medium acid, Mediterranean style (5-15 years)

Getting started: begin with Barbera or Montepulciano, move on to Sangiovese, and finally explore Nebbiolo

slides.9.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.9.points.0: ✓ Nebbiolo is Italy's greatest red grape: pale garnet in colour yet very high in tannin + acid; Barolo (king) / Barbaresco (queen) need 10-30 years to peak
slides.9.points.1: ✓ Sangiovese is Italy's most widely planted red grape, high in acid with medium-high tannin; Chianti / Brunello di Montalcino cover the full quality spectrum from everyday to top level
slides.9.points.2: ✓ Barbera is Italy's everyday star, high in acid and low in tannin, easy and versatile; Barbera d'Asti DOCG is the benchmark, and it ranks among the best-value Italian grapes
slides.9.points.3: ✓ ⚠️ A must-learn name trap: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo (the Montepulciano grape from Abruzzo) ≠ Vino Nobile di Montepulciano (a Tuscan place name + the Sangiovese grape)
slides.9.points.4: ✓ Montepulciano has medium tannin, medium acid and full fruit, an excellent-value grape — great wines at friendly prices
slides.9.points.5: ✓ Nero d'Avola is the king of Sicily, heat- and drought-tolerant, rich with Mediterranean black fruit and chocolate; Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG is Sicily's only DOCG
slides.9.points.6: ✓ A beginner's path: Barbera / Montepulciano (smooth and easy) → Sangiovese (medium structure) → Nebbiolo (top, age-worthy)
slides.9.points.7: ✓ The defining trait of Italian reds: natural high acidity, a natural match for pasta with tomato sauce, grilled meats, cheese and other Italian food
slides.9.points.8: ✓ The geographical span of the five grapes: Piemonte (Nebbiolo + Barbera) → Tuscany (Sangiovese) → Abruzzo (Montepulciano) → Sicily (Nero d'Avola)
slides.10.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
slides.10.questions.0.question: Which description best explains the character of Nebbiolo?
slides.10.questions.0.options.0: A. Low tannin and low acid, fruity, best drunk young
slides.10.questions.0.options.1: B. High acid and high tannin, but a pale ruby colour with a brick-orange rim
slides.10.questions.0.options.2: C. High acid and high tannin, inky and opaque in colour
slides.10.questions.0.options.3: D. Low tannin and high acid, fresh and easy
slides.10.questions.0.explanation: Nebbiolo's paradox: high acid and high tannin (great power), yet a pale ruby colour that develops a brick-orange rim with age. Its tannins are very astringent when young and need long ageing to soften to their best.
slides.10.questions.1.question: Which statements about Sangiovese are correct? (Select all that apply)
slides.10.questions.1.options.0: A. Italy's most widely planted red grape
slides.10.questions.1.options.1: B. High acid and medium-high tannin
slides.10.questions.1.options.2: C. Key wines: Chianti and Brunello di Montalcino
slides.10.questions.1.explanation: Sangiovese is Italy's most widely planted red grape, known for high acidity and medium-high tannin, and is the core grape of Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino and others. It is grown mainly in central Italy and is rare in Piemonte.
slides.10.questions.2.question: What is Barbera's place in Italian wine?
slides.10.questions.2.options.0: A. A premium, age-worthy wine that needs over ten years
slides.10.questions.2.options.1: B. A high-acid, low-tannin everyday wine of excellent value
slides.10.questions.2.options.2: C. The richest grape, suited to fortified wine
slides.10.questions.2.options.3: D. Mainly used for sparkling wine
slides.10.questions.2.explanation: Barbera is known for high acidity and low tannin, full of fruit (blackberry, black plum) and drunk young; it is the backbone of Piemonte's everyday wines, lively in character, and one of the best values among Italian grapes.
slides.10.questions.3.question: What is the key difference between Montepulciano d'Abruzzo (a wine) and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano (a wine)?
slides.10.questions.3.options.0: A. They are exactly the same, only the names differ
slides.10.questions.3.options.1: B. The first is the Montepulciano grape from Abruzzo; the second is from the Tuscan town of Montepulciano and made from Sangiovese
slides.10.questions.3.options.2: C. The first is in Tuscany; the second is in Abruzzo
slides.10.questions.3.options.3: D. Both the grape and the region are the same
slides.10.questions.3.explanation: A classic name trap! Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is a red wine from the Montepulciano grape in Abruzzo; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is a wine from the Tuscan town of Montepulciano whose core grape is Sangiovese (locally Prugnolo Gentile).
slides.10.questions.4.question: Which statements about Nero d'Avola are correct? (Select all that apply)
slides.10.questions.4.options.1: B. Rich and generous, with ripe black fruit and chocolate
slides.10.questions.4.options.2: C. A signature grape of northern Italy
slides.10.questions.4.options.3: D. Performs well in the hot Mediterranean climate
slides.10.questions.4.explanation: Nero d'Avola is Sicily's most famous red grape; it ripens fully in the hot Mediterranean climate and makes rich, generous reds with ripe blackberry, prune and cocoa. It is a signature grape of the south, not the north.
